And I think that's going a little too far. The fact of the matter is, there's a big difference between a judge ordering possession of a home to a spouse after there's been a violent act, which is what the senator from Eastern Fairfax was referring to when he talked about due process, and someone bringing a petition and the individual that's the subject of the order not having the right to appear in court

and defend themselves. And that's what I object to. And that's what I objected to when this bill was passed before. There is an ex parte hearing. An ex parte hearing. The person who is a subject of the order does not appear until after someone goes into house. Will the gentleman yield for a question? Will the senator from King George yield? I'll yield. Senator from Charlottesville.

Will the gentleman agree with me that a temporary detention order can issue from an ex parte hearing. Senator from King George. Madam President, typically yes. Senator from Charleston. Would the gentleman yield for an additional question? I will yield. Will the senator yield? Would the gentleman agree with me that the temporary detention order results in an involuntary commitment and an involuntary commitment can result in an indefinite loss of firearm possession? Senator from King George. I think that's accurate. Thank the gentleman. And Madam President, I would say

that that is another entirely different burden when somebody has or is temporarily detained as a result of that hearing and it is completely different from someone who makes an allegation I mean in this case you could have a divorced spouse who could make an allegation against you because that's being added and they don't like you so they can make this and then law enforcement comes into your home without your knowledge or permission and searches your home and takes your guns and whatever else they see in plain

view. It is the lack of due process that so many of us have objected to. Why can't you just give people a hearing in the beginning? Why can't they just have a hearing, have their day in court like we fight for in everything else? Now we have people who can bring this petition that don't even have a relationship with the person they're trying to get in order. I mean, I get it. A licensed clinician, all these people. But the bill doesn't say that you have to have a relationship with

the person. It just says they can bring a petition. I think it's irresponsible and I hope we don't vote for it. The chair recognizes the senior senator from Loudon. Madam President, speaking to the bill. Senator has the floor. Thank you, Madam President.

Madam President, I raised to speak in support of this bill. I was a prosecutor in the Loudon County Commonwealth Attorney's Office when substantial risk orders became effective here in the Commonwealth of Virginia, so I remember them very well as I was the sole and single person designated to prosecute them in Loudon County. I remember at the time I was also sat on our mental health document and worked extensively with folks in the criminal justice system who you know suffered and struggled with mental health issues and who we diverted on to those dockets to try to deal with them I also happen to be the person in the

Commonwealth Attorney's Office the person at the time who ended up being tasked with responding to phone calls about children who were making threats or of concern to shoot up their schools madam president and so I think in a lot of ways this bill brings home a lot of the a lot of the experience that I had then and then after I left the Commonwealth Attorney's Office and maybe the only person this body who had the privilege of sitting as a special justice resided over a mental health commitment hearings oh and I forgot when

I was a prosecutor I was the person who went to our Sheriff's Office Loudoun County Sheriff's Office and several other police departments and taught on substantial risk orders and taught on the senator from Charlottesville and the work that he was doing long before I knew him, Madam President. And Madam President, I think it's fair to say that I have first-hand knowledge of a lot of these issues. And Madam President, whether we're talking about protective

orders which are issued on a basis temporarily without a hearing, first the emergency protective order, then the temporary protective order before we get hearing for the permanent protective order. There's due process built in every single step of those cases and those cases kick people out of their homes, those cases decide children's custody, whether or not one parent can see or talk to their other children at all, and those orders take away people's firearms rights. They do all of those things and all of those things can be done without a hearing with the other person present to argue about the facts

of that case. That happens every single day here in the Commonwealth of Virginia. Madam President, would the senator yield for a question? Madam President. Will the senator yield? Madam President, if I could finish, I'm happy to answer every single question that the senator from King George County has. The senior senator has the floor.

Thank you, Madam President. Madam President, I will also say, with emergency commitment orders, individuals can come on, not just law enforcement, members of someone's family can come and petition a person, ex parte, a petition a person, and that person's going to be important, petition a person for an order that that has that person then transported for a mental health evaluation that same person that we rely on to make these sorts of decisions also makes decisions about whether or not search warrants should issue to go into people's houses that same person makes decisions about and and the person

for whom the search warrant is being issued against is not present in those hearings that person has the ability to make decisions about whether or not someone is free to be on bond or whether they will be held madam president that person is a magistrate and we trust them to make all kinds of decisions here in the Commonwealth of Virginia and so when I hear things like well you know people are gonna come in this could be innuendo this could be speculation we just don't know madam president this could be out of control it's unclear to

me if we're not gonna trust them in this situation why it is that we would possibly trust them in all of those other situations where those same types of rights sometimes the exact same rights are on the line and when we talk about lack of due process madam president when I prosecuted substantial risk orders in the Commonwealth Attorney's Office I'm just gonna point to I remember every single time that one happened what a scramble it was because the Commonwealth was responsible for not later than 14 days after the issuance of an emergency substantial risk order having a hearing and for us in the Commonwealth Attorney's Office 14 days was a short turnaround time to get

the folks present in court to protect the right to confrontation to make sure that that person had a hearing on whether or not a substantial risk order should be issued or not. 14 days is a very short time. That's shorter than the time for a temporary protection order or the exact time for a temporary protective order where there is no usually confrontational right where the other person is present, Madam President.

And so I would suggest not only are the statistics on substantial risk orders that they are a way to save people's lives. Yes, children at school and other people, suicides, family members, not only have the studies shown that they are an effective way to do that, but I would suggest that this bill and what substantial risk orders does has at least as many procedural protections as other mechanisms that we have in the Commonwealth of Virginia, Madam President.

Madam President, with that, I'm happy to yield to whatever questions my friend the senator from King George County has. Senator from King George. Thank you, Madam President. I would ask the senator, I listened to the examples about court granting custody of the home to a spouse, temporary detention order, and those others.
But is it not true in a substantial risk order The court is ordering that the individual's home be searched prior to a hearing in court by that individual in order to retrieve their firearms.

Senior Senator from Loudoun. Madam President, Senator from King George County, yes, yes, yes to the senator. I think the answer is generally yes, that there will be an effort to remove whatever firearms are at issue in that case.

I believe there's another bill that has been passed out by the Senate this year that I think does sort of similar things as it relates to making sure that folks who have had a protective order issued against them are otherwise not permitted to have firearms, that people can go in and search for those firearms.

And I will also add that whenever I prosecuted these types of case, my law enforcement officers took it very seriously as they were the best people in these types of very volatile situations to go in, not a family member, not a member of the public, to go in and to remove these firearms that were causing the danger and the concern.

And so they did it with a tactical ops plan and doing all the things they could to make sure that not only the person who was causing the risk, but the other folks who were potentially at risk were protected as much as we possibly could. Madam President. I thank the senator, Madam President.
